reference.source: OMIM / GeneReviews (NCBI) and standard clinical genetics texts
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive DNA-repair disorder caused by variants in ERCC6 (CSB) or ERCC8 (CSA), which impair transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair
Cardinal features are profound postnatal growth failure and progressive microcephaly with neurological deterioration
A cachectic appearance with deep-set eyes, prominent ears and a thin beaked nose gives a characteristic aged facies
Cutaneous photosensitivity is common, but unlike xeroderma pigmentosum there is no marked increase in skin cancer
Progressive sensorineural hearing loss and pigmentary retinopathy frequently develop
Neuroimaging classically shows calcification of the basal ganglia and cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, with leukodystrophy
Subtypes span from severe early-onset (type II) to classic (type I) and milder later-onset forms
Diagnosis combines the clinical phenotype with a DNA-repair functional assay and molecular confirmation of ERCC6/ERCC8 variants
reference.pathophysiology: Cockayne syndrome results from biallelic variants in ERCC6 or ERCC8, whose protein products are essential for transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair. Failure to remove transcription-blocking DNA lesions leads to stalled RNA polymerase, impaired gene expression and increased cellular vulnerability to oxidative and ultraviolet-induced damage. The resulting neuronal and oligodendrocyte dysfunction drives the progressive neurodegeneration, demyelination and growth failure that define the condition.
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing for ERCC6 and ERCC8 variants
Functional DNA-repair assay (recovery of RNA synthesis after UV exposure) on cultured fibroblasts
MRI brain for basal ganglia calcification, cerebral and cerebellar atrophy and leukodystrophy
Audiometry for progressive sensorineural hearing loss
Ophthalmological review for pigmentary retinopathy, cataract and optic atrophy
Growth monitoring and assessment of feeding and nutritional status
redFlags: Rapidly progressive neurological regression or intractable seizures
Severe failure to thrive with feeding difficulty and aspiration risk
Marked visual or hearing deterioration affecting development
Signs of renal or hepatic impairment as part of multisystem decline
reference.prognosis: The condition is progressive and life-limiting; the severe early-onset form is often fatal in early childhood, while the classic form typically leads to death in the first or second decade. Care is supportive and multidisciplinary, with sun protection to limit photosensitivity.
pitfalls: Mistaking the intracranial calcification for congenital infection
Confusing photosensitivity with xeroderma pigmentosum and expecting a high skin-cancer risk
Overlooking progressive hearing and visual loss that are amenable to supportive intervention
Failing to recognise milder later-onset forms because growth failure is less striking
references: OMIM: Cockayne syndrome A and B
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists; care is supportive and multidisciplinary, with early palliative involvement given the progressive, life-limiting course
Strict photoprotection with high-factor sunscreen, protective clothing and sun avoidance to limit cutaneous photosensitivity
Nutritional support for growth failure and feeding difficulty, escalating to nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding
Correct sensory deficits: hearing aids for progressive sensorineural loss and ophthalmological management of cataract, pigmentary retinopathy and optic atrophy
Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and orthopaedic care for spasticity and contractures, with anticonvulsants for seizures
Avoid metronidazole, which has been associated with acute hepatotoxicity and death in Cockayne syndrome
Surveillance for hypertension and for renal, hepatic and dental complications as the disorder progresses
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive ERCC6/ERCC8 disorder, with carrier and prenatal testing offered to the family
